overview: Venice joined lagoon engineering to a far-reaching artistic culture. This chapter follows the city and its painters during the Renaissance; it does not yet cover the republic's entire history.

items.text: During the republic, canals connected settlements consolidated from lagoon islands. Hydraulic and architectural work continually reshaped the relationship between the city and its surrounding water.
In sixteenth-century Venice, Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto developed influential approaches to painting. Their work later shaped artists including Rubens and Velazquez.
After moving from Verona in the 1550s, Veronese found both civic and church commissions in Venice. Artistic employment crossed religious and governmental settings.
The lagoon included fishing settlements and artisan communities such as Murano. Venice's palaces were part of a larger landscape of work and settlement.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Sixteenth-Century Painting in Venice and the Veneto
